newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood says Taleban must cede Kabul to U.N. force.
newsitem.headline: Masood says Taleban must cede Kabul to U.N. force.

text.p: Ousted government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood called on Friday for Taleban fighters to withdraw from Kabul and turn the Afghan capital over to a U.N.-supervised force or face war.

"We want the Taleban to evacuate Kabul," he told Reuters in the strategic town of Jabal os-Siraj. "A limited international force under U.N. supervision should control Kabul and pave the way for all-party talks on a broad-based government."
Masood, who had been standing in a street giving orders to his commanders, made clear the alternative would be war.
"If the Taleban are not ready to cooperate with us, we cannot avoid fighting," the renowned guerrilla chief said.
Masood, a Tajik, would not say if troops of his old rival, Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum, had entered the battle on his side against the radical Islamic Taleban movement.
Witnesses said Dostum tanks and infantry, pouring down from the Salang Pass at the edge of his territory, had deployed well south of Jabal os-Siraj, but were not yet at the front line.

"In our agreement with Dostum, the most important point is the formation of a broad-based government, which should avoid fighting in Kabul and prepare the ground for peace and elections in Afghanistan," said Masood.
Three weeks after its forces took Kabul promising peace and security, the Islamic Taleban movement were thus facing an apparently united military front north of the capital.

Together Masood and Dostum present a formidable foe to the Taleban, purist Moslems whose leaders have vowed to rid Afghanistan of the "evil and corrupt forces" which they say are behind the country's long-running civil conflict.
But behind the scenes Dostum was still talking peace with the Taleban, leaving many in Kabul in suspense over whether the ravaged city was in for another devastating siege or not.

A three-man delegation sent by Dostum to Kandahar, the Taleban's southern stronghold, on Thursday agreed to continue talks started in the north a day earlier under the auspices of Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar.
A Taleban spokesman said afterwards he was hopeful an understanding between the two sides could be reached.
In the shifting alliances of Afghan politics, few tried to guess which way Dostum, a former communist general who controls six of Afghanistan's northern provinces, would jump.

"Deployment and talks are not necessarily inconsistent. Dostum is clearly making himself the key to a deal and his deployment just strengthens the pressure on the Taleban," one veteran Afghan watcher in Kabul said late on Thursday.

The Taleban took Kabul on September 27 after a lightning campaign, bringing a measure of security and peace back to areas under its control, as well as imposing a strict brand of Islam which bars most women from working or learning.
The military situation remained unclear on Friday.

Jeep-loads of turbanned Taleban fighters have been rushed out of Kabul in recent days to battle for control of Bagram military airbase and the nearby junction of the two roads leading out of the capital, the main focus of fighting.
Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of the city, remained in Taleban hands, travellers said.
Refugees fleeing the area said the Taleban had been burning houses, apparently to deter local people from attacking their rear as they try to push back Masood's forces.
They also said two Masood commanders, Anwar Dangar and Amanullah Quchi, had switched sides on Thursday, bringing with them valuable forces in key areas of the frontline.
Both commanders are Pashtu speakers, as are the mainly Pashtun Taleban, whose heartland is in the south of Afghanistan. Masood and Dostum have their strongholds in the north.
It was not immediately possible to confirm the report.
Kabul was quiet, although fighting to the north has forced hundreds of refugees to flee to both sides of the frontline.
The conflict has raised alarm among neighbouring countries. India and Iran, both accused by the Taleban of interfering in Afghanistan, called on Thursday for an end to the fighting.

President Farooq Leghari of Pakistan, whose country has been brokering peace talks between Dostum and the Taleban, was due to fly to the Uzbek capital Tashkent on Friday to reassure Central Asian states that the Taleban had no territorial ambitions.
Islamabad has denied charges it backs the Taleban, a movement born in the refugee camps of Pakistan two years ago.
